attacks.claim: The weekly public CC-BY export publishes per-response ward, zip, birth_year, gender, created_at and ranking. Removing resident_id does not prevent re-identification from these quasi-identifiers, especially in small zip/ward cells. The plan has no suppression, generalization (e.g. age bands), or k-anonymity control, and the disclosure is irreversible once published. It also conflicts with the anonymous-first constraint.
attacks.evidence: "one CSV per poll on data.ourtown.org with columns ward, zip, birth_year, gender, ranking, verified, created_at. resident_id is removed before export."

attacks.claim: Demographic data collected at optional verification for demographic balance reports is repurposed into public ballot exports and staff reports. The plan documents no notice or consent for this new use. The same data flow also couples the poll system to identity data.
attacks.evidence: "collected at optional verification for the jury-pool-style demographic balance reports" vs. "Open-data export (weekly, public, CC-BY)"

attacks.claim: The plan buys the county voter file and sends automated SMS to ~142,000 registered voters, plus 3 reminders, who never opted in to OurTown. It documents no consent basis, which creates TCPA exposure. Voter files are commonly use-restricted by state law or Clerk terms, and no license or data-use review is noted. It also contradicts the anonymous-first, opt-in premise. Sent messages cannot be recalled, and no staged rollout, dry run, or kill switch is described. STOP-only handling does not cure missing consent.
attacks.evidence: "Purchase the county voter registration file from the County Clerk ($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)." / "send an automated SMS to every registered voter in the city (~142,000) ... then 3 automated reminders over 10 days." / "Reply STOP handled by Twilio's default opt-out."

attacks.claim: Imported voter-file records (names, addresses, phones) are loaded into the DB and Twilio with no stated retention or deletion schedule, access control, credential handling, or processor terms. Device fingerprints and IPs are also collected with no disclosure or retention rule. Responses are immutable with no erasure path.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention period, deletion schedule, access restrictions, or credential storage for the purchased voter file; "Staff cannot edit or delete responses"

attacks.claim: The 142k-recipient SMS pipeline has no throttling, idempotency, send-state tracking, retry, or resume logic. A mid-campaign failure could cause double-texting or silent partial delivery. The burst also drives a traffic spike onto the self-hosted app and Postgres that the 5k-concurrent load test is not tied to. No launch monitoring or alerting is specified, nor is any rollback or abort procedure for launch.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: idempotency, retry policy, send-state tracking, monitoring, or abort procedure; "Week 5: accessibility pass, load test (target 5k concurrent), launch."

attacks.claim: There is no cost model for the SMS campaign: roughly 568k outbound messages plus carrier and 10DLC fees. Reminders are unconditional and go to everyone regardless of engagement, with no spending ceiling. Only the $400 voter-file purchase is priced.
attacks.evidence: "then 3 automated reminders over 10 days"; "($400, includes mobile numbers where provided)"

attacks.claim: The centerpiece feature is not supported by the plan's own survey: polls ranked last at 9%, while voting records (61%), neighborhood notifications (44%), and plain-language summaries (37%) go unaddressed. There is no council commitment to act on results. The 6,000-response target has no derivation. The reach figure of ~142,000 ignores that mobile numbers exist only 'where provided'. The 'direct voice' framing overstates what advisory results deliver.
attacks.evidence: "Polls on upcoming items — 9%" vs "is the centerpiece of the FY27 roadmap"; ABSENT: any basis for expected response rate or council commitment

attacks.claim: Integrity controls are weak. Dedup relies on a client-controlled device fingerprint, and over-limit IP traffic is only queued, with no defined review state or release path. Self-selected ward values from unverified users go unvalidated into per-ward results.
attacks.evidence: "1 response per poll per device fingerprint + 1 per verified resident; unverified responses over 3/min from one IP are queued for review."; "ward is self-selected for unverified users"

attacks.claim: Live IRV results are recomputed over all responses with no caching or materialization. The weekly export and PDF are unbounded full reads on the same self-hosted servers that serve the live app. This is a risk under launch load.
attacks.evidence: "Live results page: instant-runoff rounds, split into \"verified\" and \"all responses\" columns."

attacks.claim: Staff-authored option text flows into the public CSV and the emailed PDF with no stated escaping, so it is exposed to spreadsheet formula injection.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: sanitization or CSV/formula escaping for options and ranking outputs

attacks.claim: The drag-or-tap ranking UI has no stated keyboard or screen-reader alternative. No WCAG target is set, and accessibility is deferred to a single week-5 pass.
attacks.evidence: "Week 2: resident ranking UI (mobile-first, drag or tap-to-rank)." / ABSENT: any WCAG conformance target

attacks.claim: Scope is not credible for 3 people in 5 weeks. Week 4 bundles the export, PDF, voter-file import, and SMS pipeline, and the load test falls in week 5 with no slack for fixes.
attacks.evidence: "Week 4: open-data export, staff PDF, voter-file import + SMS pipeline."
